Guides

How the meal happens

What you serve is your decision. Whether it is eaten, and how much, is the child’s. Pressure is a poor teacher.

Findings

Use a division of responsibility. The adult chooses the food, the time, and the place. The child chooses whether to eat and how much.
A refused food usually needs more calm exposures, not a replacement meal. Eight to fifteen tastings, without pressure, is a normal arc for a new flavour.
Screens, aeroplane spoons, and dessert bargains backfire. They teach a child to ignore hunger and to treat sweet food as the prize.

Who decides what

Ellyn Satter’s division of responsibility is the cleanest statement of responsive feeding. You offer a structured meal that includes something the child usually accepts and something they are learning. You sit down. You do not plead, chase, or make a second lunch when the first is refused.

A baby who turns away, clamps the mouth, or plays is done. Ending the meal then is a success. It is how they learn that their own fullness counts.

Repeated exposure

Food neophobia, a suspicion of new foods, rises in the toddler years and is ordinary. The evidence-based response is repeated neutral exposure: the food appears, nobody comments much, and it comes back next week. Praise for eating, and disappointment for refusing, both add pressure.

Short-order cooking, in which a refusal produces a favourite alternative, trains the refusal. Serve one meal. Include a safe food so the child will not leave hungry. Let the new food be ignorable.

Tricks that are not worth it

Feeding while a screen distracts the baby fills the stomach and skips the lesson. Bribes (‘finish this and you may have something sweet’) make the savoury food the chore. Hiding every vegetable so thoroughly that a child never sees it also skips the lesson. A visible piece, even if it is left, is doing work.

Eat together when you can. Children copy the people at the table more reliably than they follow a speech about healthy food.
